questions.explanation: “Before” locates the detection in time relative to degradation becoming routine.
optionExplanations: It does not express why degradation occurs.

support.summary: English connectors are often tested through their logical relation in context.
support.example: “Detect the problem before it spreads” sets a time relation.

stimuli.label: Text 1
stimuli.text: A predictive model can be highly accurate on historical data and still fail in production. The reason is not always a defect in the algorithm. Customer behavior may change, sensors may be replaced, or the way a field is recorded may be altered. When the statistical properties of incoming data shift, monitoring must detect the change before performance degradation becomes invisible routine.
stimuli.source: Original passage written for this simulation.

questions.prompt: Which sentence preserves the meaning of “Customer behavior may change”?
options: Customer behavior is forbidden to change.
Customer behavior changes only after monitoring.
Customer behavior used to change but no longer does.
It is possible that customer behavior changes.
questions.explanation: Modal “may” expresses possibility in this context.
optionExplanations: The passage gives no such condition.

support.summary: May often signals possibility; must signals necessity; should usually signals recommendation.
support.example: “The distribution may shift” = “It is possible that the distribution shifts.”
support.trap: FGV may exploit Portuguese speakers’ tendency to confuse modal strength.

When production data stop resembling the past

questions.explanation: The text is about changes in incoming data and the resulting need for monitoring.
optionExplanations: Sensor replacement is only one example.
The text does not promise elimination of all errors.

support.example: “When production data stop resembling the past” captures data shift and its consequences.
support.trap: Options built from a vivid example are tempting but usually too narrow.

questions.prompt: The main point of Text 2 is that
options: data lakes should contain only processed data.
storage capacity automatically creates analytical value.
governance can support, rather than undermine, sustainable flexibility.
raw data should never be preserved.
ownership and lineage reduce trust in data.
questions.explanation: The final sentence states the core thesis: governance is not opposed to flexibility; it makes flexibility sustainable.
optionExplanations: The passage explicitly mentions preserving raw information.
The text says storage alone does not create value.
It describes preserving raw data as a legitimate goal.
Ownership and lineage are presented as factors that increase trust.

support.summary: Pay attention to “therefore”, which often introduces the author’s conclusion.
support.example: Flexible storage without governance may scale ingestion while reducing trust.
support.trap: The distractor may repeat the opening motive but miss the author’s conclusion.

stimuli.label: Text 2
stimuli.text: Organizations often create a data lake because they want to preserve raw information for future use. Yet storage alone does not create analytical value. If datasets have no ownership, catalog, lineage, or quality rules, the lake may become easier to fill than to trust. Governance is therefore not the opposite of flexibility; it is what makes flexibility sustainable.
stimuli.source: Original passage written for this simulation.

questions.prompt: In “the lake may become easier to fill than to trust”, “trust” most nearly means
questions.explanation: In context, trust is confidence that the data are reliable enough for use.

support.summary: Trustworthy data are data users can reasonably rely on.
support.example: A dataset may be easy to access but hard to trust if its origin and quality are unknown.
support.trap: Technical contexts can narrow a common word’s meaning.
